turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hey, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Look, I’m a pretty busy guy, right? I run my own company, built it from the ground up after I left high school, so I’m used to having a million things on my plate and managing a lot of moving parts. But what made me actually make this appointment and come in today is that for the past year or so, it’s just been getting ridiculous. 

I’ll be sitting at my desk, trying to look over some numbers or deal with a vendor, and the absolute smallest thing just completely derails me. Like, my phone will buzz on the desk. Not even a ring, just a tiny vibration—maybe it’s a spam email, maybe it’s a text—and before I can even tell myself not to look at it, I’ve already picked it up and lost my train of thought. Or, you know, my office has these big glass walls, which I thought was a great idea for company culture, but if somebody just walks past my office, maybe carrying a coffee or talking to a manager, boom, I’m watching them, wondering what they're up to, completely forgetting what I was just reading. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around the office. It’s in my own head, too. I’ll be right in the middle of a serious task and I’ll get this completely random thought about my in-laws. Just out of nowhere, I'm sitting there wondering if my father-in-law is going to bring up politics at the next family dinner, and it just pulls me off what I’m doing before I can even stop it. It’s like my brain just gets hijacked by whatever tiny thing happens to cross my path, and it's been driving me crazy for a year now.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly describes being easily derailed from tasks by extraneous stimuli (a phone buzzing, people walking by) and unrelated thoughts (random thoughts about his in-laws).

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood, say around elementary or middle school, did you struggle with these same kinds of focus and distraction issues back then?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s funny you ask that, because... yeah. Yeah, absolutely. Looking back, this was definitely happening around when I was a kid, too. I was actually just thinking about this the other day, remembering my fourth-grade teacher—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was. She was always, and I mean constantly, moving my seat. It became like a running joke, honestly, because I just talked way too much. I’d be put next to one kid, start a full-blown conversation about whatever movie I saw that weekend while she was trying to teach fractions, and then boom, I’m moved to the back of the room. Then I’d just start talking to the kid back there. 

And it wasn't just the talking, either. I was the kid who would just... get up without asking. Like, if I needed to sharpen a pencil, or if I just wanted to see what was on the bulletin board, or if I dropped an eraser, I wouldn't raise my hand and wait for permission, I’d just stand up and walk over there. It drove the teachers absolutely up the wall. They'd always be stopping the lesson to tell me to sit back down. 

And the questions! Man, if a teacher was asking the class something, I would just blurt things out before they even finished the sentence. I wouldn't even mean to be disrespectful, it was just like... the answer popped into my head and my mouth was already saying it before my brain could hit the brakes. Like I couldn't hold it in if I tried. So yeah, elementary school, middle school, it was always the exact same story at every parent-teacher conference. 'He's a chatterbox, he won't stay in his chair, he interrupts.' They tried putting my desk literally attached to the teacher's desk at one point, right up at the front of the chalkboard, just to keep an eye on me, because I just couldn't sit there quietly and wait my turn like the other kids. Sitting still was just pure torture for me back then, which is probably half the reason I didn't stick around to finish high school, to be honest.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes frequently getting up without asking and not staying in his chair during class.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient notes that sitting still was 'pure torture' for him, indicating a strong feeling of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states he 'talked way too much' and was called a 'chatterbox' by teachers.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient mentions he would 'blurt things out before they even finished the sentence.'
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient states he 'couldn't sit there quietly and wait my turn like the other kids.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient recalls teachers noting at parent-teacher conferences that 'he interrupts.'

turns.doctor_question: In your day-to-day life as an adult, do you still find yourself feeling physically restless, like you need to be constantly moving, or do you find that you frequently act on impulses without thinking things through?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it’s not exactly like I’m jumping out of my seat to look at a bulletin board anymore, but that feeling? It hasn't gone anywhere. It’s just... it’s still there, 100 percent. Especially when I’m in a situation where I am really, strictly supposed to just sit still and be quiet. 

Like, okay, take family dinners for example. My wife’s family does these big, long, drawn-out sit-down dinners, and I swear, ten minutes into the appetizer, I am already crawling out of my skin. Or, I do this church volunteer thing—they roped me into the finance committee because of my business background, right?—and we have these monthly meetings in this tiny, stuffy little conference room where everyone just talks in circles for an hour. 

And I’ll be sitting there in one of those awful folding chairs, and it literally feels like there is a motor running inside of me. Just this constant, humming engine that will not shut off. I can't just get up and pace around the room like I do in my own office, so I end up absolutely needing to move or do something with my hands just to burn off that energy. I’ll be shredding my paper napkin into a million tiny pieces under the table, or I’ll take my pen completely apart, springs and all, and put it back together five times while the pastor is talking. My wife actually has to kick me under the table at those family dinners because I’ll start bouncing my leg so fast that the water glasses start shaking. If I don't have something to do with my hands, or if I can't move at least a little bit, that internal motor just revs and revs until I feel like I'm going to explode. So yeah, the physical restlessness is definitely still a huge thing for me.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes needing to do something with his hands, shredding napkins, taking pens apart, and bouncing his leg.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly confirms experiencing intense physical restlessness, especially in situations where he is expected to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling like there is a 'motor running inside' of him and a 'constant, humming engine that will not shut off'.

turns.doctor_question: In your daily life, aside from the restlessness you mentioned, do you frequently make careless mistakes in your work or lose items necessary for your tasks because you were distracted?
turns.patient_response:
Actually, no, not really. I mean, you'd think so, right? With how my brain bounces around and how I can't sit still, you'd assume I'm just leaving a trail of disaster behind me, but I'm actually pretty dialed in when it comes to the actual output and keeping track of my stuff. 

Take the work mistakes, for example. I don't make careless errors. You just can't run a successful company—especially one you built from the ground up with no college degree to fall back on—if you're dropping the ball on the numbers or signing bad contracts. I check my work. If I'm looking at an invoice from a supplier, say, the guys who provide our raw materials out in Ohio, I might get distracted by a text message or a truck backing up outside, exactly like I was telling you earlier. But when I look back down at the paper, I'm reading it right. I'm not approving the wrong quantities or missing a zero. I'm actually very particular about that. If anything, I probably double-check things just to make sure, but no, I'm not making silly mistakes on the actual work. 

And as for losing things? No, never. I have a very strict system for my personal items. Keys go in the front left pocket, phone in the front right, wallet in the back right. Always. Every single day since I was a teenager. If I take my sunglasses off, they go right into the center console of my truck, nowhere else. I don't just set things down randomly. I mean, honestly, my wife is the one who's always losing her stuff. Just last week, we were supposed to go over to her sister's house—the one with the father-in-law I mentioned before, the one who always wants to argue about politics—and we spent twenty minutes tearing the kitchen and the living room apart because she left her car keys in the laundry room on top of the dryer. I don't do that. My stuff is always exactly where it needs to be. I might be tapping my foot a hundred miles an hour while I grab my keys off the hook, but I always know exactly where they are. So, no, I wouldn't say I make careless errors or lose my things at all.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient admits to being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like text messages or trucks backing up outside.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes tapping his foot 'a hundred miles an hour', indicating fidgeting.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient mentions that he 'can't sit still', confirming feelings of restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly denies making careless errors or silly mistakes in his work.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly denies losing things, stating he has a strict system for his personal items.
